interactions.summary: Jiang reopens a prior class question and distinguishes ego from pride by contrasting a Kabbalah account of ego as bodily desire with Dante's account of ego as a divine potential that can be perverted into pride.
He resets a disputed explanation of Dante's treatment of homosexuality and says the right way in is to interpret the punishment pattern first rather than begin with modern categories.
A student tentatively links the punishment to pride and superiority, and Jiang accepts that as partial progress while pressing for the group dimension of the punishment.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student answer followed by Jiang prompt

interactions.summary: Students and Jiang move from pride to a more specific answer: the punishment pattern points to factional or mafia-like behavior, where people only serve their own group at the expense of society.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student attempts with Jiang steering the logic

interactions.summary: Jiang answers his own prompt by introducing the idea of a 'gay mafia': persecuted homosexual networks secretly helping one another rise inside bureaucracies instead of merit alone deciding status.
Students sharpen Jiang's model by linking secret coordination to taboo-breaking bonds and to harsher punishment for betraying the group's vow.

Jiang extends the argument: once one elite network can accumulate power through factional coordination, rival factions form, inequality rises, ordinary people are pushed toward fraud, and society slides toward lawlessness.
A student remains unconvinced about why homosexuality would enable faction-building more than heterosexuality, forcing Jiang to restate the mechanism.
A student tries to reconcile Inferno and Paradiso through a family-versus-individual distinction, and Jiang endorses that as part of the explanation.
Jiang restates his mechanism by opposing heterosexual marriage as an exclusive pair-bond to male homosexual networks he says can spread across multiple lovers and become institutionally powerful.
Students test Jiang's model by recasting homosexuality as a secret-society mechanism with hierarchy, then question whether the same logic still holds under modern openness and acceptance.

Jiang updates the argument from medieval text to contemporary politics, claiming decadent elites no longer hide corruption, that family-centered restraint has collapsed, and that modern identity variants follow the same self-indulgent logic in Dante's terms.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang answer with student follow-up question

interactions.summary: Jiang closes the disputed homosexuality section by saying modern LGBT variants follow the same self-indulgent logic in Dante's frame, then pivots to the practical limits of free inquiry under livestreaming, censorship, and cross-cultural scrutiny.

A student asks whether voluntary childlessness should fall under the same logic, and Jiang answers by detouring through celibate Catholic prestige and the brutal material conditions that made medieval childbirth a life-and-death issue for women.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student question, Jiang reply, student elaboration, Jiang expansion

interactions.summary: A student proposes an Aristotelian telos account of lust versus homosexuality, and Jiang answers by separating Aristotle's social-purpose telos from Dante's more individual and intuitive understanding of purpose.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student question followed by Jiang answer

interactions.summary: A student asks how sacred artistic inwardness differs from narcissism, and Jiang corrects his own previous framing by saying the real problem is factionalism, not self-indulgence itself.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student question followed by Jiang correction

interactions.summary: The class begins Canto 21, where the bolgia of graft is imagined as sticky boiling pitch policed by violent black demons who seize corrupt officials.
The reading of the grafters continues and Jiang glosses the bolgia as the fraud circle where corrupt officials stew in punishment and are shredded whenever they try to escape.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading followed by Jiang explanation

interactions.summary: Virgil hides Dante, confronts the demons alone, and secures a temporary stay by invoking divine authorization before Malacoda.
Jiang asks what is new here, and the class identifies two surprises: demons now actively administer punishment, and Dante is hiding because Virgil himself is afraid and less in control.
Jiang and the students analyze Virgil's fear: he protects Dante, then copes with his own anxiety by posturing before the demons and leaning on higher authority, which Jiang reads as a pride response.
A student asks why Virgil is not simply master of hell, and Jiang answers that hell is like Italy: a pride-ridden field of rival powers where Virgil's control shrinks as he descends.

Jiang answers a student question about how the demons know Virgil can be fooled by building a real-life bazaar analogy: pride makes a person advertise control, and that visible need to save face is exactly what a trickster exploits.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student prompt followed by Jiang explanation

interactions.summary: The canto reading shows Dante physically returning to Virgil while the demons close in, and Jiang glosses Dante's bodily fear through the same bazaar analogy of knowing the deal is unsafe while the proud guide keeps insisting he has it under control.

The reading presents Malacoda's false reassurance and Jiang underlines that any explicit promise of harmlessness inside the fraud circle should itself be heard as a warning sign that Virgil misses because of arrogance.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading followed by Jiang interpretation

interactions.summary: The canto stages the escort of ten demons, Dante's explicit request to avoid them, Virgil's reassurance, and the grotesque comic signal from the demon leader.

Jiang asks why Dante now openly challenges Virgil, and the class works through fear, frustration, and Virgil's pride before Jiang stresses the real novelty: Dante finally speaks his distrust aloud instead of silently submitting.

A student proposes that Dante may be surpassing Virgil, but Jiang rejects that frame and instead interprets Dante's protest as an act of love that risks hurting Virgil's pride in order to protect him, which lets the journey become a love story rather than a mere lesson in cosmology.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student proposal with Jiang's extended answer

interactions.summary: Another student reads the scene as a truth-versus-lie urgency, but Jiang disagrees again and argues that Dante must linger in hell because the poet's vocation is to experience punishment deeply enough to report it back to the world.
A student reads Dante's grotesque military-comic scene of the demon escort, the boiling pitch, and a grafter from Navarre being hooked up and questioned about his birthplace and office.
Jiang pauses on the unusual punishment and asks why grafters are given repeated chances to pop out of the pitch and try to escape, and students begin to answer in terms of compulsion and addiction.
Jiang accepts the student's idea of compulsion but pushes for a more exact mentality: grafters repeatedly could turn back yet keep choosing the theft.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student answer with Jiang refining the question

interactions.summary: Students propose benefit without punishment, entitlement, pride, and a difference from greed, while Jiang keeps steering the class toward graft as theft rooted in a position of power.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led discussion with multiple student answers

interactions.summary: Jiang shifts from generic stealing to the concrete case of a servant stealing from a generous lord, and students answer in terms of disrespect, rejection of hierarchy, and a belief that tribute entitles the subordinate to take more.

Jiang resolves the question by defining the grafter's mentality as 'I'll get away with it': the sinner keeps taking the risk of escape, gets torn apart, resurrects, and repeats the same confidence forever.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang explanation with brief student clarification

interactions.summary: The canto continues with the wounded Navarrese sinner naming other grafters, then offering to whistle more sinners out of hiding if the demons will momentarily stand back.

Jiang glosses the scene as fraud stacked on fraud: the sinner deceives demons who enjoy tearing people apart, the demons fall for it and crash into the pitch, and Jiang asks the class to name the deeper paradox behind that lie.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading with Jiang interpretation and prompt

interactions.summary: Jiang rejects a superficial answer about demonic punishment and reframes the issue as a paradox of technically truthful but manipulative language, using the sinner's statement to define sophistry rather than simple lying.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student answer followed by Jiang explanation

interactions.summary: A student asks whether the sinner is really trying to escape hell, and Jiang answers that the deeper impulse is compulsive cheating rather than a coherent escape plan.
The class resumes the canto as Dante and Virgil move on to the next bolgia under the shadow of the frog-and-mouse fable.
Jiang pauses the canto to recover Aesop's frog-and-mouse fable from a student summary and then maps it onto the demons, who become victims of their own treachery and greed.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang prompt, student summary, then Jiang gloss

interactions.summary: The reading shows Dante and Virgil fleeing the devils, with Virgil carrying Dante down the embankment like a mother saving a child while providence limits the demons' reach.
Jiang asks why Dante includes a danger scene whose outcome is already guaranteed by providence, and a student answers that the point is comradeship.
Jiang answers that the chase scene exists to deepen the relationship between Dante and Virgil, turning shared danger into intimacy and character-building.
The canto introduces the hypocrites in glittering lead cloaks, identifies the jovial friars, and culminates in Caiaphas stretched on the ground where everyone walks over him.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading Dante with brief identification gloss

interactions.summary: Jiang explains the punishment of hypocrites and asks the class to define hypocrisy, beginning with the student's answer that it is saying one thing and doing another behind a mask.
Students link hypocrisy to superiority, false moral display, and cheating others for advantage, while Jiang sharpens the issue by stressing the emptiness and opportunism of unbound words.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Students answering Jiang's prompt with Jiang synthesis

interactions.summary: Jiang uses a teacher-student example to show hypocrisy as saying the right things to please authority or harvest benefits, and the class answers that the resulting lies eventually become a weight on consciousness, which Jiang maps onto the cloak punishment.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang example with student responses and Jiang conclusion

interactions.summary: The canto resumes as Virgil asks the friars for a usable route and hears that the devils misled him about the bridge.

Virgil realizes he trusted false directions, the reading names the devil as a liar and father of lies, and Jiang converts the mistake into a diagnosis of pride: trusting the devil comes from overconfidence.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang gloss, student reading, then Jiang interpretation

interactions.summary: The canto shifts into a winter-farmer simile and then stages Virgil driving Dante up the broken bridge while exhorting him to cast aside laziness and pursue fame.
Jiang pivots from Virgil's rhetoric to a live classroom analogy about teachers who justify soul-crushing study regimes by promising worldly greatness.

Jiang asks whether the class has known teachers who preach hardship now for future benefit, and one student answers that this is ordinary teacher talk about present bitterness leading to later sweetness.
A teacher in the room openly says she gives students a 'six years of hell or sixty years of hell' bargain and Jiang confirms that this approach often does produce students who reach top universities.
Jiang then opens the floor for dissenting perspectives rather than closing the issue with the success narrative alone.

One student calls meritocratic schooling an endless trap, Jiang tests that claim against another student who still believes in the hard-work narrative, and the counterargument links it to a Puritan-Christian reward structure.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student critique, Jiang prompt, student counterargument

interactions.summary: Another student says instrumental teacher rhetoric only tells her how much effort is required for the grade, whereas genuine love of a subject evokes real effort because education should better the self and remain enjoyable.
Further students shift the issue from hard work itself to motivation and then question the premise that career and income are the only goods worth organizing a life around.

Jiang keeps taking final comments as students successively describe the educational success narrative as self-blinding, a generationally repeated white lie, and a boredom-producing failure to teach why learning matters.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang invites closing responses; multiple students answer

interactions.summary: A final student pushes back that learning cannot be built on passion alone because many necessary disciplines are painful, and some larger future-oriented narrative is still needed to keep students working outside their favorite subjects.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang gives the last word; student counterargument follows

interactions.summary: Jiang supplies context about China's six-subject comprehensive exam and then returns to Dante, arguing that Virgil's fame-based motivation is psychologically weaker than invoking Beatrice.
Jiang concludes that Virgil's psychology is exposed by his choice to motivate Dante with fame instead of with Beatrice, whose presence would move Dante more directly.
The canto moves into the thieves' bolgia with serpents, burning metamorphosis, Vanni Fucci's theft confession, and his political prophecy against Pistoia and Florence.
Jiang interrupts to ask why theft is placed lower in hell than large-scale violence, stressing the paradox that a conqueror can sit above a thief.

A student reaches for the Ten Commandments and coveting as a way to explain theft, but Jiang presses the opposite conclusion: biblical hierarchy seems to rank theft relatively low, which sharpens rather than resolves Dante's paradox.

Another student proposes that hidden crimes receive harsher treatment because they are harder for society to detect, but Jiang replies that this cannot explain Dante at the divine level because God already sees everything.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student answer followed by Jiang objection

interactions.summary: A student proposes that theft violates natural law as well as divine law because even animals fiercely defend property, and Jiang endorses that point as a useful angle.

Another student argues that theft destroys future love and trust because hidden violation makes everyone suspicious, and Jiang turns that into his main explanation: the deepest damage is to the social fabric required for faith, hope, and love.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student answer, Jiang elaboration, student clarification, Jiang synthesis

interactions.summary: A student adds that thieves deceive themselves as well, and Jiang answers that the snake punishment externalizes how theft leaves a venomous imprint, generates false accusations, and makes society obsess over hidden betrayal.
A student connects the thieves' serpents to Genesis and Jiang agrees, treating the snake as an explicit reminder of the primal trust-break between God and Adam and Eve.
A student asks why Dante uses the phoenix, a seemingly positive image, for sinners, and Jiang answers that the simile is visual rather than moral: it shows repeated burning and rising, not approval.

The reading shows Fucci cursing God, Jiang asks why he hates God so much, and a student answers that thieves may not grasp the full social damage of their acts and therefore experience the punishment as unjust.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading, Jiang prompt, student answer

interactions.summary: A student clarifies that a thief may not grasp the scale of the harm while committing the crime, and Jiang answers that Fucci's rage comes from believing he had staged a perfect crime until God intervened and ruined it.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student clarification with Jiang follow-up and answer

interactions.summary: Jiang pauses for logistics, announcing an early Thursday session with David Bromwich for a Shakespeare-and-Dante comparison, and confirms a student question about the morning schedule.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang announcement with brief student question

interactions.summary: After lunch Jiang restates the central paradox of the canto: Dante treats a thief who breaks communal trust as worse than Alexander's mass killing, and Jiang says Paradise is needed to explain why.
Jiang answers the genocide-theft paradox by arguing that bodily death matters less than damage to the soul's ability to live in faith, hope, and love.

A student reads Dante's extended metamorphosis sequence for the thieves, including Cacus, the six-footed serpent, body-merging transformations, and the closing identification of the unchanged Puccio Sciancato.
Jiang glosses the canto as identity theft and asks why Dante unusually dwells on metamorphosis in exhaustive detail rather than moving on quickly.

Students speculate that the long metamorphosis description may contrast hell's microscopic restriction with heaven's expansiveness, dramatize dehumanization, or let Dante compete openly with Ovid on metamorphosis.
Jiang affirms student ideas about Ovid and Revelation, then adds that Dante may be stretching out the metamorphosis scene to generate horror and dread as readers approach Lucifer.
The reading moves into Canto 26: Dante prophesies doom for Florence, then approaches the fire-filled abyss where each flame encloses a sinner.
The reading identifies the twinned flame of Ulysses and Diomedes, and Jiang explains that Dante's Ulysses comes through later writers and is punished with Diomedes for Trojan-horse treachery.
Virgil addresses the flame, Ulysses narrates his final voyage beyond Hercules' boundary in pursuit of knowledge, and Jiang highlights the paradox that such longing still ends in hell.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading with Jiang interpretive synthesis

interactions.summary: Students propose that Ulysses either flees purgatory or tries to seize godlike knowledge; Jiang accepts the purgatory-avoidance angle but rejects the stronger claim that this is the same as explicitly wanting to be God.

A student points out that Ulysses explicitly places wandering above father, son, and wife; Jiang answers that this is exactly the failure, because exploration without family love as an anchor becomes rootless ambition.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student observation with Jiang answer and follow-up question

interactions.summary: Jiang continues the Ulysses discussion by arguing that individuality is socially anchored, then answers why Ulysses is worse than thieves or murderers: he betrays roots, family roles, and even the conditions that make identity possible, which is why exile is felt as identity death.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang answer to student question with student follow-up

interactions.summary: A student returns to the serpent image and links it to the original serpent robbing Adam and Eve of paradise, and Jiang strengthens the link by noting Milton's devils also end as snakes.

A student reads the simile of the Sicilian bull and Jiang explains why Dante chooses it: not to treat the flame as abstract decoration but to force the reader to feel the bodily agony inside the fire.

The reading moves through Guido da Montefeltro's confession: asked about Romagna's politics, Dante receives the story of a former foxlike strategist who became a friar, was recruited by Boniface VIII for fraudulent counsel, received advance absolution, and was nevertheless claimed by a black cherub because unrepented fraud cannot be absolved.
Jiang restates Guido's story and names its first paradox: Saint Francis appears ready to honor Boniface's corrupt promise of heaven until a fallen angel intervenes.
A student asks what a black cherub is, Jiang explains it as a fallen angel, and another student returns to the contradiction problem around repentance and the failed rescue.
Jiang resolves the contradiction in practical terms: declared repentance is meaningless if the actions still consist of treachery, manipulation, and deceit.

Students extend the problem to papal corruption and to manipulation as the dark inversion of love's imagination, while Jiang keeps emphasizing both Boniface's damnation and the unresolved strangeness of Francis honoring the contract.
Students keep pressing the contradiction around the fallen angel's authority, and Jiang sharpens the puzzle: why does the black cherub have priority over Saint Francis at the moment of judgment?

Jiang speculates that the pope's contractual authority must be honored because he represents God on earth, yet the canto's deeper point is that a law above church contract and office still governs salvation; students name that law justice and universal truth.
The reading opens the bolgia of sowers of discord with grotesque dismemberment and with Muhammad naming himself and Ali as split figures among those who caused scandal and division.
Jiang explains that Dante sees Islam as a schismatic offshoot of Christianity, so Muhammad and Ali become exemplary sowers of dissension in a medieval Catholic frame.

The reading continues with the devil repeatedly reopening wounds, Muhammad's message to Fra Dolcino, and other discord-sowers such as Pier da Medicina, Curio, and Mosca, each marked by the bodily form of the division they caused.
The reading presents Bertrand de Born carrying his severed head like a lantern and naming himself as the counselor who split father and son, making civil rupture visible as bodily division.
Jiang glosses the scene as counter-penalty for permanent discord and then asks the class to imagine modern equivalents for this circle.

Students propose Donald Trump and J.D. Vance as present-day sowers of discord, and Jiang accepts Trump as a plausible example because of polarization while pressing for the exact mechanism of division.
A student names J.D. Vance as another conflict-sower, and Jiang pushes back by asking whether that would make every politician equally guilty.
The conversation shifts from individual politicians to social media, and Jiang argues that algorithmic anger production makes Mark Zuckerberg a more fitting example of engineered discord.
Students float Greta Thunberg, media in general, and Nick Fuentes, while Jiang keeps narrowing the exercise toward naming concrete agents rather than abstract systems.
Students keep testing modern names and the meaning of schism, and Jiang settles on Trump as the cleanest example because the split is intra-political and not necessarily about explicit belief in God.
The reading shifts into the next canto, where Dante lingers on the mutilated shades and then explains his fixation through the unavenged blood-guilt of his kinsman Geri del Bello.
The reading enters the disease-ridden ditch of falsifiers and focuses on Italian alchemists such as Griffolino and Capocchio, whose bodies are degraded by scabs, plague, and false transformation.
Jiang identifies this lowest fraud area with alchemy and asks why trying to turn lead into gold or find immortality would be the worst fraud, prompting the class to begin the analogy work.

Students propose false hope and greed as explanations, and Jiang sharpens the answer into a metaphysical one: alchemy is worse because it tries to warp the laws of God and nature rather than merely the laws of society.
A student explicitly compares AI to old alchemy, and Jiang immediately endorses the analogy while extending it to nuclear energy.
Students test moon travel and AI's practical benefits, while Jiang says moon travel is not alchemy but still a troubling Ulysses-like attempt to exceed natural limits.
A student tries to distinguish AI from the internet, Jiang insists the internet is not alchemy, and he challenges the class to articulate the difference.

Jiang makes the wordplay case that artificial intelligence is inherently alchemical, and a student connects that claim to a larger course warning about manipulating reality as if humans could replace divinity.

Students extend the analogy to artificial insemination and genetic engineering, and Jiang answers an AI skepticism objection by saying Dante would judge the intent to create God or immortality rather than the current technical success.

A student argues that splitting the atom is unlike impossible alchemy because it is actually within the fabric of the universe, while Jiang keeps the focus on entering dangerous foundational territory.

Jiang answers by treating money as a successful human workaround for turning paper into gold and by insisting that where there is will and imagination, the sinful drive to distort order can still find an outlet.

Students restate alchemy as the will to replace God or betray created nature, and Jiang closes the discussion by saying even failed alchemy breeds hubris because it persuades people that natural law can be overwritten.

The reading opens canto 30 with mythic madness, then shows violent falsifiers such as Myrrha and Gianni Schicchi attacking others in beast-like frenzy before turning to the bloated body of Master Adam.
The passage then centers on Master Adam's thirst, his counterfeit florins, and his filthy quarrel with Sinon, before Virgil rebukes Dante for taking too much pleasure in the bickering.

Jiang re-sorts canto 30's confusing cast of falsifiers, proposes that the section is too intentional to be a mere garbage heap, uses Gianni Schicchi's attack on a leper as a clue to punishment logic, and then asks why Master Adam and Sinon are enraged at being grouped together.

Students propose that counterfeiters, spies, and impostors all alter reality by preying on trust, and Jiang accepts the line of thought, especially the idea that these sins attack larger civilizational trust rather than isolated personal exchanges.

The class pushes beyond ordinary theft and alchemy toward a higher-order fraud: falsifiers manipulate souls, trust, and history itself, and Jiang responds by asking for the missing key term that explains how they succeed where alchemists fail.

After a student offers consciousness or imagination, Jiang proposes his main solution: the falsifiers are united by hijacking imagination itself, which lets him identify modern influencers and voice-fraud systems as especially dangerous forms of social power.

The reading enters the giant circle: Dante mistakes giants for towers, Virgil explains the error, Nimrod howls in Babel gibberish, Iphialtes is chained for rebelling against Jove, and Antaeus is named as the speaking giant who can lower the travelers further down.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading Dante aloud with one Jiang gloss

interactions.summary: Antaeus physically lowers Dante and Virgil into the pit that holds Lucifer and Judas, making the descent to Cocytus depend on giant mediation.

Jiang notices a structural symmetry between angels guiding ascent in paradise and giants guiding descent in hell, then accepts student suggestions about fear, irony, and heaviness before proposing that giants materially express the rocky substance of hell itself.

Jiang and the students deepen the giant-angel analogy through weight, silence, harmony, and discord, and Jiang explicitly praises the class for helping him imagine something he had not seen on his own.
The reading opens canto 32 with a fearful invocation equal to the melancholy pit where the circles of hell converge.
Jiang says the music contrast matters because heaven is pure song while hell also has music, but only in the form of sighing, groaning, melancholy, and despair.
The reading enters the frozen lake at the base of the universe, where the lowest souls lie beneath the giants' feet.

Jiang closes by emphasizing the shocking paradox of a frozen hell and a not-quite-kingly Lucifer, previews the next day's Inferno conclusion and Purgatory start, and thanks the class for a seminar in which he also learned from their individuality.

claims.claim: Jiang says Kabbalah treats the ego as the bodily husk and its material desires, while Dante treats the ego as a divine spark or potentiality rather than something simply bad.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive comparison made in class on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: He argues that for Dante pride is the perversion of ego because it seeks superiority and subordination over other people, which cuts a person off from equality, trust, and access to God.
Jiang presents Virgil as Dante's classic embodiment of pride rather than a purely neutral guide.
He says the proper method for understanding Dante's punishment of homosexuals is to start from punishment as God's perfect justice and infer the social pattern it answers.
claims.temporal_scope: Method statement in this lecture on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang says the group punishment should be read as punishment for factionalism, fraternity, or mafia-style loyalty where a group advances itself by harming or excluding others.
He argues Dante's ideal society is meritocratic at the individual level, but real societies are often captured by people who can conspire together in secret.
claims.temporal_scope: Model of social order discussed on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang says persecuted homosexuals may help one another obtain success in secret and that this hidden mutual aid is what lets them become a bureaucracy-controlling 'mafia' in his reconstruction of Dante's logic.
He cites imperial China, the Vatican, Washington, and Hollywood as recurring examples for his claim that homosexual networks rise high within bureaucratic systems.
Jiang accepts the student's suggestion that taboo-breaking can generate a stronger bond and that leaving the network would therefore trigger a harsher punishment for violating the group.
He argues heterosexual marriage is structurally narrower because loyalty is confined to a pair, whereas male homosexual networks can expand into broader reciprocal group ties.
Jiang says once one faction amasses power, other groups are forced to form rival factions, producing elite conflict, resource monopolization, inequality, fraud, and finally lawlessness.
He says the real issue for Dante is not homosexuality in isolation but what Jiang thinks homosexuality leads to socially: bureaucratic capture, moral decay, corruption, and factional rule.
The student argues that healthy family order serves the individual, whereas the corrupt pattern under discussion is a group using itself to elevate particular members.
Jiang says heterosexual marriage is a compact between only two people, so adding more lovers breaks the bond rather than expanding it into a wider faction.
A student and Jiang distinguish lesbians from male homosexuals, suggesting that the latter are the case Jiang thinks can sustain multiple-lover networks that turn into social power.
Jiang says the intention of homosexual networks is not evil in itself; persecution drives them into secret-society behavior that can then solidify into hierarchy and institutional infiltration.
He argues that once a society becomes decadent, elites cease caring about family or social reproduction and instead openly indulge desire without responsibility to the broader society.
Jiang uses Donald Trump and a hypothetical Democratic return in 2028 to argue that rival elites will intensify corruption rather than restore republican virtue.
claims.temporal_scope: Prediction and diagnosis made on 2026-06-24 about 2028 U.S. politics.

claims.claim: He says earlier societies at least required elites to honor family publicly, whereas current openness can coincide with a deeper indifference to society's long-term health.
Jiang says Dante would make no distinction between homosexuality and LGBT variants here because the underlying issue is self-indulgence without concern for social impact.
He says a livestreamed global seminar in China requires privacy caution and self-censorship because contemporary culture judges speech harshly and censorship is now a pervasive reality.
claims.temporal_scope: Current media and speech diagnosis on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang contrasts his college-era norm of free speech as a primary ideal with a present culture of cancellation and harsh punishment for speech.

He argues that voluntary childlessness cannot be treated simply in medieval terms because celibate religious figures were revered and because childbirth for women in Dante's era involved extreme risk, including a high chance of death.
Jiang states that Beatrice died in childbirth at age twenty-four and uses that as a concrete reminder of how deadly reproduction was for women in Dante's world.
The student frames lust as mismeasured desire toward an otherwise proper reproductive telos, while homosexuality is presented as missing the reproductive telos altogether.
Jiang says Dante would know Aristotelian telos but diverges from Aristotle by treating true purpose as something to be discovered inwardly rather than simply assigned by society's expectations.
He distinguishes between society exploiting a person through an imposed telos and a person actually understanding and achieving a genuine telos.
Jiang explicitly revises his earlier explanation and says the problem in Dante is not self-indulgence but factionalism; a degree of self-love and ego is necessary for creating great art.
The reading of Canto 21 introduces grafters and corrupt officials submerged in boiling pitch and hunted by demons, shifting the lecture from the homosexuality dispute into the bolgia of graft.
claims.temporal_scope: Narrative turn in the lecture on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang defines the current bolgia as the fraud circle for grafters, where corruption and simony are punished by immersion in boiling filth and renewed torment when the damned try to surface.
Virgil tells Dante to hide and then confronts the demons by appealing to divine will and helpful fate rather than by sheer force.
Jiang says this is the first time in the poem Dante is hiding, which reveals that Virgil is now afraid in a way the earlier hell encounters did not force into the open.
Jiang says Virgil, though bodiless, still has emotions; otherwise hellish punishment would be unintelligible.
He argues Virgil responds to fear by becoming proud and arrogant before the demons, effectively flexing rather than admitting uncertainty.
Jiang says Virgil may be master of some regions of hell but not all of them, and that deeper descent means less control because hell is internally factional rather than a unified kingdom.
He interprets the demons' compliance as suspicious because the circle of fraud is built on deception; their obedience is likely the first move in a trick against Virgil.
Jiang says the demons can see that Virgil's pride makes him want to display mastery, which is why they judge him easy to deceive.
He argues arrogant people are easier to trick than humble people because they are invested in maintaining face and control.
claims.temporal_scope: General model stated in class on 2026-06-24.

claims.claim: Jiang reads Dante's huddling near Virgil as evidence that Dante already senses the escort arrangement is dangerous even while Virgil keeps projecting confidence.
He treats Malacoda's line that there is 'no malice' in the demon escort as a classic fraud tell: the verbal assurance itself is evidence that trickery is coming.
Jiang repeats the lecture's chronology that the broken bridge dates back to Christ's descent into hell, which is why the demons redirect Dante and Virgil.
Jiang says Dante verbally challenges Virgil here in a way he has not done before, even though he has felt unease in earlier episodes.
He presents Virgil's pride as a practical obstacle because Virgil insists on the complicated escort arrangement instead of taking the simpler safer exit Dante wants.
Jiang frames Dante's speech as a threshold event because fear is no longer merely inward intuition; it becomes spoken resistance to Virgil's judgment.
Jiang says Dante's warning to Virgil is an act of love rather than a claim to superior knowledge, because Dante is risking conflict with Virgil in order to protect him.
He argues the real story of the journey is the growth of affection between Dante and Virgil, so the poem should be read as a love story as well as a theological map.
Jiang says the poem prepares readers to weep at the eventual separation between Dante and Virgil by steadily deepening their mutual affection.
He rejects the idea that Dante should hurry out of the realm of liars and instead says Dante must experience hell as fully as possible so he can return and tell others the truth about sin.

claims.claim: Jiang frames graft as a crime in which the sinner could return what was taken at many points but instead keeps choosing the illicit gain.
The class distinguishes graft from simple greed by tying it to entitlement and misuse of position rather than only desire for a particular object like money.
Jiang implies that pride is involved in graft because the thief privately decides the stolen thing is more properly his than the owner's.
Jiang links graft to a refusal to honor a legitimate hierarchy or benefaction: the grafter steals from the very lord whose trust or generosity created the opportunity.
He defines the grafter's core mentality not as need but as clever impunity: 'I'm smarter than you, and I'll get away with this.'
Jiang says the punishment fits because grafters repeatedly choose the worse outcome, preferring another impossible try at escape over accepting the lesser pain already assigned to them.
He describes the punishment as eternal repetition: the sinner is torn apart, re-forms in the pitch, and immediately resumes the same delusion of getting away next time.
Jiang says everyone in this bolgia should be treated with suspicion because it is the circle of fraud and deception, so even apparently helpful speech is probably a trick.
He reads the sinner's proposal to summon seven more grafters as a tactical lie that exploits the demons' appetite for more victims.

Jiang introduces a rule of hell for this discussion: when damned souls address Dante and Virgil directly, their words are supposed to be true, which creates a contradiction when this sinner appears to lie.
The packet's paradox is that demons get punished for believing a liar in the realm of fraud, while the liar seems momentarily to succeed by manipulating their own violent instincts.

Jiang says the sinner's statement to the demons is not a direct lie but a technically true sentence designed to be misread, which lets Dante preserve the rule that damned souls speaking to Dante and Virgil cannot simply lie.
He defines sophistry here as verbal manipulation that hides behind technically defensible wording while exploiting other people's interpretation.
Jiang argues the sinner's impulse is not genuine freedom-seeking but an addictive need to prove he is smarter than everyone else by cheating them again.
The apparent escape is itself part of punishment because the fraudster keeps choosing the compulsive pattern that traps him.
Jiang reads the frog-and-mouse fable as a miniature of the demon episode: the demons try to swindle Dante and Virgil, become greedy for more victims, and end up caught by their own trap.

The chase scene is narratively unnecessary at the level of plot protection because providence already guarantees Dante's survival, but Jiang treats it as meaningful at the level of relationship-building.
Jiang says the ordeal with the demons is there to build intimacy between Dante and Virgil, much as external danger can turn rivals into companions.
The hypocrites are punished by heavy lead cloaks whose glittering exterior and crushing interior mirror the split between appearance and reality.
Jiang treats Caiaphas's punishment as fitting because the figure who advocated sacrificing one man for the nation is now literally stretched under everyone's feet.
The student's starting definition of hypocrisy is that it means saying one thing and doing another while presenting a false image of moral superiority.
Jiang synthesizes hypocrisy as speech detached from responsibility: words that can be changed at will because the speaker is using them instrumentally rather than truthfully.
The social motive for hypocrisy is to please authority, appear superior, and gain benefits without doing the inner work the words claim.
Jiang accepts the student's formulation that lies must eventually be worn on the self, which is why the cloak of lead externalizes the burden that hypocrisy once hid.
The new narrative turn is that Virgil discovers the devils gave false directions about the bridge out of the bolgia.
Jiang interprets trusting the devil as a manifestation of pride, because only a proud person assumes he can safely bargain with or outsmart a liar.
Virgil's motivational language in the climb centers on fame, renown, and overcoming bodily heaviness through spirit.
Jiang analogizes Virgil's speech to teachers who demand extreme sacrifice by promising future prestige and institutional immortality.
The classroom confirms that a severe delayed-gratification narrative is standard educational rhetoric: endure six bad years now so the rest of life will be better.
Jiang does not deny that this motivational strategy can work instrumentally; he explicitly notes that many students do reach elite universities through it.
The packet frames the live debate not as a factual dispute about outcomes but as a deeper dispute about what kind of motivation education should use.
A student diagnoses meritocratic schooling as an endless trap in which every reward only renews the command to grind for the next credential or job.

The debate expands from method to life-philosophy when students challenge the assumption that money, banking, and elite status are the right measures of a good life.

Students characterize the dominant educational script as self-blinding or a generational white lie whose usefulness depends on audience and whose danger is fixation on the wrapping rather than the substance.
Another student argues that education fails when students are told only to chase school, college, and jobs instead of learning why knowledge is enjoyable and intrinsically valuable.
The counterargument is that passion alone is insufficient because comprehensive education requires painful effort across subjects one may not naturally love.

claims.claim: Jiang says Virgil's psychology is exposed by the way he motivates Dante with fame rather than with Beatrice, even though Beatrice is the actual object of Dante's desire and the more effective source of movement.
Jiang says Virgil could motivate Dante more effectively by invoking Beatrice instead of eternal fame, which reveals Virgil's own worldview and motivational limits.
The thieves' punishment joins serpents, incineration, and repeated reconstitution, with Vanni Fucci identified as a church thief whose crime also caused someone else to be blamed.
Jiang frames the placement of thieves as a real paradox: Dante ranks theft below spectacular violence even though theft can seem situationally understandable.
The Ten Commandments do not straightforwardly justify Dante's ranking because theft appears there as a lower-order prohibition compared with direct offenses against God.
One student's secular explanation is that hidden crimes are punished more severely because their secrecy makes them harder for human judges to discover and deter.
Jiang rejects detectability as the final explanation because God does not face human evidentiary limits and therefore cannot be fooled by hidden crime.
A student's natural-law angle is that theft is deeply disruptive because even animals enforce boundaries around possession and are intensely reactive to stealing.
Jiang's main explanation is that theft is terrible because hidden stealing destroys social trust, forces generalized suspicion, and can redirect blame onto innocent people.
For Dante, society is not peripheral to religion; it is the medium within which faith, hope, and love can actually be lived.
Jiang reads the snake punishment as a metaphor for the thief's social effect: slippery hidden injury, lingering venom, obsessive suspicion, and misdirected retaliation.
Jiang says the serpent imagery in the thieves' bolgia deliberately recalls Genesis and the original breach of trust between God and humanity.

Jiang announces that David Bromwich will join the Thursday session for a live comparison of Shakespeare and Dante, requiring an earlier class start.

Jiang frames Dante's paradox as follows: a thief who destroys trust in a community of roughly a thousand people is treated as committing a worse sin than Alexander's glory-driven conquest that killed millions.

Jiang says the million dead are not the decisive moral issue because bodies perish while souls continue; the graver damage is communal betrayal that makes faith, hope, and love harder to live.
For Jiang's Dante, the worst sin is treachery that pressures other people into treachery and thereby drives them away from God.

claims.claim: Jiang says this lowest area of the circle of fraud is reserved for alchemists.
Jiang defines alchemy as the attempt to turn lead into gold or to discover an elixir of youth or immortality.
Jiang frames the real puzzle not as whether alchemy is wrong at all, but why Dante would treat it as the worst fraud compared with theft, identity fraud, or heresy.

Jiang agrees with the student analogy that AI counts as alchemy.
Jiang also classifies new nuclear energy as alchemy in the same broad sense of manipulating the deep structure of reality.
Jiang says the moon landing is not alchemy, but he still treats it as Ulysses-like overreach against the laws of nature and the proper moral order.
Jiang continues to classify AI and nuclear energy as alchemy even while distinguishing them from moon travel.
Jiang draws a categorical line between the internet and AI by saying the internet is not alchemy.
The student counterargument defines the internet as spreading ordinary worldly ideas, while AI is framed as creating something from nothing.
Jiang says the phrase 'artificial intelligence' is itself enough to identify AI as alchemy because it names the artificial making of intelligence.
Jiang says the contemporary world assumes there are no moral laws at work and behaves as though humans can become their own God in a post-truth condition.
Jiang agrees that artificial insemination and genetic manipulation aimed at producing perfect offspring also count as alchemy.
Jiang answers the objection that current AI is only a tool by saying Dante would focus on intention: Silicon Valley is trying to create God or immortality even if it never succeeds.
Jiang says nuclear energy counts as alchemy because it enters the most fundamental fabric of nature without knowing the consequences of the act.
Jiang uses money as an analogue for successful alchemy by saying human beings already turn paper into gold-like purchasing power through symbolic intermediaries.
Jiang argues that Dante's real concern is not literal metallurgical success but malicious will joined to imagination, because where there is a will there can be a way around formal impossibility.
A student reinforces Jiang's line by linking alchemy to Tower-of-Babel ambition: the will to replace God and distort natural order repeats whenever humans keep pressing impossible projects.
A student formulates the issue as the will to replace God and distort the natural order he established.

Jiang says alchemists are sinful even when they fail because they make others believe the rules of nature can be changed, which produces hubris and bad behavior.
Jiang says he wants to keep using Dante to interpret present issues, especially AI.

claims.claim: Jiang defines canto 30 as a zone of falsifiers that includes alchemists, impostors, counterfeiters, false witnesses, and related figures such as Sinon, Master Adam, Gianni Schicchi, and Myrrha.
Jiang rejects the idea that this canto is a random dump-site for miscellaneous sinners, because Dante's arrangement is too intentional for that.
Jiang treats Gianni Schicchi's attack on a leper as meaningful because at that time lepers were precisely the people everyone wanted to avoid, so the impostor is forced into degrading contact.
Jiang says the quarrel between Master Adam and Sinon comes from their rage at being together despite being different types of falsifiers.
Jiang accepts the student's formulation that Master Adam and Sinon are alike because both manipulate people's perception of reality rather than reality itself.
Jiang analogizes Sinon to a fake-news reporter, making false witness a modern media problem rather than just an ancient military trick.
A student's answer, which Jiang invites, is that all these sinners prey on trust.
The stronger version of that argument is that these falsifiers manipulate large social trust, such as money or the destiny of an entire civilization, not just one interpersonal exchange.
A student argues, and Jiang affirms, that these falsifiers go a step beyond alchemy because they manipulate ensouled beings and social identities rather than mere objects.
Another student names the pattern as a kind of false or meta-trust, a higher-order theft that operates at the level of confidence itself.
The class explicitly contrasts alchemists, who cannot really change nature, with falsifiers, who do succeed in changing human belief and the course of events.
Jiang signals that the key explanatory term for this success is a concept central to both today's and yesterday's lecture, which the next packet identifies as imagination.
Jiang identifies imagination, not consciousness in general, as the crucial category that explains what the falsifiers share.

Jiang's theory is that falsifiers hijack imagination for evil ends: counterfeiters hijack value, spies hijack truthfulness, impostors hijack authorship of identity, and all thereby contract the universe rather than expanding it.
Jiang says that, on this reading, the worst modern figures would be influencers or people with huge followings because they hijack social consciousness or social imagination.
Jiang adds that in America media workers can hold unusually strong power, which makes this hijacking dynamic socially consequential at scale.
The AI voice-fraud example is accepted by Jiang as proof that modern fraud works by impersonating intimate voices and hijacking the imagination of millions of people at once.
The canto stages an interpretive mistake in which distance makes giants look like city towers until Virgil corrects Dante's faulty image.
The reading presents giants as creatures whose combination of acute intelligence, evil will, and massive power makes ordinary human defense impossible.
Jiang glosses Nimrod as the builder of the Tower of Babel and says his punishment is incomprehensible speech.
The reading distinguishes chained rebel giants like Iphialtes from Antaeus, who is unchained and able to carry Dante and Virgil down toward Cocytus.
Jiang highlights a deliberate symmetry: angels guide the journey upward in paradise, while giants guide the journey downward into the final circle of hell.
Jiang says Dante gives no settled answer for why giants rather than other beings guard this threshold, forcing readers to use imagination.
Jiang's own best guess is that giants are made of clay and rock just as hell is, while angels are made of divine light just as heaven is.
A student's accepted extension is that sin becomes heavier and heavier like a snowball falling into the abyss.
Jiang develops the heaviness analogy by saying sin can keep reproducing itself until it becomes a giant.
A student suggests that giants are largely silent while angels are musical, so heaven elevates the soul into harmony whereas hell collapses it into numbness and silence.
Jiang warmly endorses that interpretation and says Divine Comedy works by exciting the imagination rather than by providing fixed explanatory footnotes.
A student etymologically links discord to the opposite of accord or harmony, reinforcing the musical contrast between heaven and hell.
Jiang says hell has its own kind of music, but it is music of sighing, groaning, melancholy, despair, and apathy rather than heavenly singing.
Jiang presents the frozen lake at the center of hell as one of Dante's most revolutionary paradoxes because readers expect fire and brimstone instead.
Jiang says Lucifer will prove not to be the straightforward king of hell that readers expect.
